The question of whether freezing kills yeast in dough is genuinely contested across the retrieved sources. One source claims outright that "it kills the yeast and defrosts the dough during the freezing process" [d1], while another directly contradicts this, stating "if the yeast was alive when you froze the bread dough, freezing it won't kill the yeast" [d2]. A forum discussion similarly presents both views, with one user reporting their dough failed to rise after freezing, while another states that "yeast and cheese cultures are not killed by freezing them" [d3].

The most credible source, Modernist Cuisine, offers a nuanced finding: "freezing temperatures do not kill all the yeast and lactic acid bacteria in a preferment. Some die, but most remain dormant while frozen," though eventually ice crystals grow large enough to damage yeasts and render them useless for leavening [d10]. This is consistent with practical baking evidence, which notes that "freezing will kill some of the yeast," which is why commercial producers "double or even triple" the yeast amount in dough intended for freezing [d8]. Sources describing successful freezing of shaped rolls and dough that still rises after thawing further support the view that yeast is not entirely destroyed [d5, d7, d9].

In summary, freezing does not kill all yeast in dough — most yeast cells survive in a dormant state — but some yeast does die, and prolonged freezing (beyond roughly two weeks) can cause increasing damage via ice crystal formation [d10]. The outcome depends on yeast type, freezing duration, and technique, with instant yeast generally tolerating freezing better than sourdough yeasts [d6].
